section_summary: The section opens with Japanese temporary currency legislation and a diplomatic assessment of financial conditions in North China. It then records Japanese gold holdings and a series of gold shipments to the United States in 1938–1939. The final, continuing report analyzes Japan’s gold exports, consumption, reserves and production.

subfiles.title: Temporary Currency Law, Law No. 86
subfiles.about: Authorizes temporary subsidiary coins and fifty-sen paper money.
subfiles.summary: The law sets coin denominations and legal-tender limits, permits fifty-sen paper money, and assigns its issue and conversion to the Bank of Japan.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 387: Temporary Currency Law in Chosen, Taiwan and Karafuto
subfiles.about: Extends the Temporary Currency Law to Chosen, Taiwan and Karafuto.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance applies the law in Chosen, Taiwan and Karafuto from promulgation.

subfiles.title: Imperial Ordinance No. 388: Forms of Temporary Currencies
subfiles.about: Specifies the composition, dimensions and designs of temporary coins and fifty-sen notes.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance prescribes metal content, weights and dimensions for ten-, five- and one-sen coins, and the size and appearance of fifty-sen paper money.

subfiles.title: Despatch on financial conditions in North China
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Embassy, Hankow
subfiles.about: Forwards a conversation memorandum and assesses possible British policy toward China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson encloses Hall Patch’s assessment of North China’s finances. He reports British uncertainty about future policy and doubts that Chamberlain’s government will give China positive assistance.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Hall Patch
subfiles.about: Records Hall Patch’s views on North China’s currency, foreign trade and wartime finance.
subfiles.summary: Patch says the new Federal Reserve Bank’s notes have not yet seriously harmed British trade, while Japanese control of export exchange would threaten foreign importers. He doubts the bank can provide a sound currency and describes financial strains in both Japan and China. He discusses possible Anglo-American sanctions, aid to China, and oil-company credits extended to Japan.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Japanese earmarked gold

subfiles.title: Reply on Japanese earmarked gold
subfiles.about: Gives the amount and custody arrangements for earmarked Bank of Japan gold.

subfiles.title: G-2 report on Japan’s gold holdings census
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, military attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes Japan’s ordinance requiring reports of privately held gold.
subfiles.summary: The report details who must declare gold coins and bullion, the reporting period and exemptions. Creswell considers the measure an effort to locate usable gold and notes uncertainty about how much earlier mobilization measures produced.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Gold Problem
subfiles.from: L. H. Gourley, American consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s gold exports, domestic use, reserves and efforts to obtain more gold.
subfiles.summary: The report’s title and contents pages outline a broad study of gold production and mobilization across Japan and its territories. In the portion present, Gourley estimates that Japan exported more than 412 metric tons of gold from March 1937 through February 1939, chiefly to the United States, while restricting domestic consumption and concealing detailed shipment statistics. He traces earlier export controls, Bank of Japan purchases and reserve declines, the 1937 revaluation of Japanese, Chosen and Taiwan bank gold, and a further reserve reduction in 1938. The report continues beyond page 160.
